claim: Dietary fatty acids are the main building blocks for cell membranes in animals.
source: Dietary fatty acids are the main building blocks for cell membranes in animals, and mechanisms must therefore exist that compensate for dietary variations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation.

claim: Eight alleles of the novel gene fld-1 were isolated that improved tolerance to dietary saturated fat in a sensitized genetic background.
source: We isolated C. elegans mutants that improved tolerance to dietary saturated fat in a sensitized genetic background, including eight alleles of the novel gene fld-1 that encodes a homolog of the human TLCD1 and TLCD2 transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: FLD-1 encodes a homolog of the human TLCD1 and TLCD2 transmembrane proteins.
source: We isolated C. elegans mutants that improved tolerance to dietary saturated fat in a sensitized genetic background, including eight alleles of the novel gene fld-1 that encodes a homolog of the human TLCD1 and TLCD2 transmembrane proteins.
evidence: This is supported by sequence homology analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: FLD-1 is localized on plasma membranes.
source: FLD-1 is localized on plasma membranes and acts by limiting the levels of highly membrane-fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipids.
evidence: This is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: FLD-1 acts by limiting the levels of highly membrane-fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipids.
source: FLD-1 is localized on plasma membranes and acts by limiting the levels of highly membrane-fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing phospholipids.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomic analysis showing increased LCPUFA levels in fld-1 mutants (Figure 3F-G).

claim: Human TLCD1/2 regulate membrane fluidity by limiting the levels of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane phospholipids.
source: Human TLCD1/2 also regulate membrane fluidity by limiting the levels of polyunsaturated fatty acid-containing membrane phospholipids.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP measurements and lipidomic analysis in HEK293 cells with TLCD1/2 knockdown (Figure 4A-C).

claim: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 do not regulate the synthesis of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids but rather limit their incorporation into phospholipids.
source: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 do not regulate the synthesis of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids but rather limit their incorporation into phospholipids.
evidence: This is supported by experiments showing no increase in desaturase expression (Figure 3C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2O) and increased incorporation of labeled LA in TLCD knockdown cells (Figure 4H-I).

claim: Inhibition of FLD-1 or TLCD1/2 prevents lipotoxicity by allowing increased levels of membrane phospholipids that contain fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids.
source: We conclude that inhibition of FLD-1 or TLCD1/2 prevents lipotoxicity by allowing increased levels of membrane phospholipids that contain fluidizing long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing suppression of SFA toxicity and increased LCPUFA levels in mutants/knockdowns.

claim: C. elegans daily replaces nearly 80% of its membrane phospholipids using mostly dietary fatty acids as building blocks.
source: For example, the nematode C. elegans daily replaces nearly 80% of its membrane phospholipids using mostly dietary fatty acids as building blocks (Dancy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dancy et al., 2015.

claim: Human AdipoR1/2 are homologs of the C. elegans PAQR-2.
source: Similarly, the human AdipoR1/2 that are homologs of the C. elegans PAQR-2, also regulate membrane fluidity in human cells (Bodhicharla et al., 2018; Devkota et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Human AdipoR1/2 regulate membrane fluidity in human cells.
source: Similarly, the human AdipoR1/2 that are homologs of the C. elegans PAQR-2, also regulate membrane fluidity in human cells (Bodhicharla et al., 2018; Devkota et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Over 100,000 mutagenized haploid genomes were screened, leading to the isolation of 15 independent mutants that suppress the glucose intolerance of the sensitized strains.
source: In all, over 100 000 mutagenized haploid genomes were screened, leading to the isolation of 15 independent mutants that suppress the glucose intolerance of the sensitized strains.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and results of the genetic screen.

claim: Eight of the 15 novel mutations that suppress SFA toxicity in sensitized C. elegans backgrounds were alleles of fld-1.
source: The fact that 8 of the 15 novel mutations that suppress SFA toxicity in sensitized C. elegans backgrounds were alleles of fld-1 suggest that mutating this gene is the easiest genetic mean to prevent this toxicity.
evidence: This is based on the results of the genetic screen.

claim: Mutating fld-1 is the easiest genetic means to prevent SFA toxicity in sensitized C. elegans backgrounds.
source: The fact that 8 of the 15 novel mutations that suppress SFA toxicity in sensitized C. elegans backgrounds were alleles of fld-1 suggest that mutating this gene is the easiest genetic mean to prevent this toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the high frequency of fld-1 alleles recovered in the screen.

claim: Introducing a wild-type fld-1 transgene abolished the suppression of paqr-2 mutant phenotypes.
source: Introducing a wild-type fld-1 transgene abolished the suppression, demonstrating that the novel fld-1 alleles are loss-of-function mutations (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the rescue experiment shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: The novel fld-1 alleles are loss-of-function mutations.
source: Introducing a wild-type fld-1 transgene abolished the suppression, demonstrating that the novel fld-1 alleles are loss-of-function mutations (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments and Western blot analysis.

claim: The FLD-1 protein is absent from the fld-1(et48) mutant.
source: Western blot assays using an antibody against a C-terminal peptide show that the FLD-1 protein is absent from the fld-1(et48) mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: FLD-1 belongs to a protein family characterized by the presence of a TLC domain.
source: fld-1 encodes a multiple-transmembrane domain protein homologous to the human TLCD1 and TLCD2 proteins (Figure 1E) that belong to a protein family characterized by the presence of a TLC domain and that includes the ER-localized ceramide synthases as well as translocation associated membrane proteins involved in membrane protein synthesis in the rough ER (Pewzner-Jung et al., 2006; Winter and Ponting, 2002).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citations.

claim: The TLC domain protein family includes ER-localized ceramide synthases and translocation associated membrane proteins involved in membrane protein synthesis in the rough ER.
source: fld-1 encodes a multiple-transmembrane domain protein homologous to the human TLCD1 and TLCD2 proteins (Figure 1E) that belong to a protein family characterized by the presence of a TLC domain and that includes the ER-localized ceramide synthases as well as translocation associated membrane proteins involved in membrane protein synthesis in the rough ER (Pewzner-Jung et al., 2006; Winter and Ponting, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pewzner-Jung et al., 2006 and Winter and Ponting, 2002.

claim: TLCD1 has been described as a positive regulator of calcium channel activity.
source: The function of TLCD1 and TLCD2 is not known, although TLCD1 (also known as calfacilitin) has been described as a positive regulator of calcium channel activity (Papanayotou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Papanayotou et al., 2013.

claim: TLCD1 is localized to the plasma membrane of mammalian cells.
source: The same study localized TLCD1 to the plasma membrane of mammalian cells using a careful series of myc-epitope tagging and immunodetection experiments (Papanayotou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Papanayotou et al., 2013.

claim: FLD-1 is expressed in the plasma membrane of most or all cells throughout development and in adults.
source: Transgenic C. elegans carrying a translational GFP reporter (Pfld-1::FLD-1::GFP) reveal that FLD-1 is also expressed in the plasma membrane of most or all cells throughout development and in adults (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplements 3C and 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by confocal imaging of transgenic worms shown in Figure 1F and supplementary figures.

claim: The Pfld-1::FLD-1::GFP reporter is functional.
source: Note that the Pfld-1::FLD-1::GFP reporter is functional since it restores the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: Expression of FLD-1::GFP in either hypodermis or intestine is sufficient to restore the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant.
source: Expression of FLD-1::GFP in either hypodermis or intestine was also sufficient to restore the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant, suggesting that fld-1 can act in a variety of tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by tissue-specific rescue experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and C.

claim: fld-1 can act in a variety of tissues.
source: Expression of FLD-1::GFP in either hypodermis or intestine was also sufficient to restore the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant, suggesting that fld-1 can act in a variety of tissues (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and C).
evidence: This is inferred from tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: The maintenance of membrane homeostasis is cell nonautonomous and may rely on effective trafficking of lipids among tissues.
source: This is consistent with an earlier study demonstrating that the maintenance of membrane homeostasis is cell nonautonomous and may rely on effective trafficking of lipids among tissues (Bodhicharla et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bodhicharla et al., 2018.

claim: The fld-1 single mutants have no obvious phenotypes and were indistinguishable from wild-type worms for brood size, pharyngeal pumping, locomotion, defecation, survival at 37°C or 30°C, length, UPRer activation, and life span.
source: The fld-1 single mutants have no obvious phenotypes and were indistinguishable from wild-type worms for the following traits: brood size, pharyngeal pumping, locomotion, defecation, survival at 37°C or 30°C, length, UPRer activation scored using the reporter phsp-4::GFP on normal media or in presence of glucose, and life span (Figure 1—figure supplement 6A–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by various phenotypic assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A-I.

claim: The fld-1 mutant shows increased activation of the oxidative stress response reporter gst-4::GFP when cultivated in the presence of linoleic acid.
source: The only phenotype that we noted in the single fld-1 mutant is an increased activation of the oxidative stress response reporter gst-4::GFP when the worms are cultivated in the presence of the LCPUFA linoleic acid (LA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6J–L), suggesting a defect in LCPUFA management in the mutant.
evidence: This is demonstrated by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6J-L.

claim: The fld-1 mutant has a defect in LCPUFA management.
source: The only phenotype that we noted in the single fld-1 mutant is an increased activation of the oxidative stress response reporter gst-4::GFP when the worms are cultivated in the presence of the LCPUFA linoleic acid (LA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6J–L), suggesting a defect in LCPUFA management in the mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased oxidative stress response in the presence of LA.

claim: All five tested fld-1 alleles suppressed the glucose intolerance, cold intolerance, and withered tail tip morphology defects of the paqr-2 mutant to a similar degree.
source: All five tested fld-1 alleles could suppress the three phenotypes to a similar degree, indicating that they are all likely null alleles (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phenotypic assays shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The five tested fld-1 alleles are all likely null alleles.
source: All five tested fld-1 alleles could suppress the three phenotypes to a similar degree, indicating that they are all likely null alleles (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar suppression effects of all five alleles.

claim: The fld-1(et48) mutation suppresses the glucose intolerance of the iglr-2(et34) single mutant and paqr-2(tm3410) iglr-2(et34) double mutant.
source: The fld-1(et48) mutation also suppresses the glucose intolerance of the iglr-2(et34) single mutant and paqr-2(tm3410) iglr-2(et34) double mutant (Figure 2C), as anticipated from the fact that paqr-2 and iglr-2 are mutually dependent for maintenance of membrane homeostasis (Svensk et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: paqr-2 and iglr-2 are mutually dependent for maintenance of membrane homeostasis.
source: The fld-1(et48) mutation also suppresses the glucose intolerance of the iglr-2(et34) single mutant and paqr-2(tm3410) iglr-2(et34) double mutant (Figure 2C), as anticipated from the fact that paqr-2 and iglr-2 are mutually dependent for maintenance of membrane homeostasis (Svensk et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Svensk et al., 2016a.

claim: Y48G8AL.13 and F41H10.5 mutants did not suppress the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant.
source: There exist four other genes in C. elegans that are closely related to fld-1 (Figure 1E), and null mutants were available for two of them (Y48G8AL.13 and F41H10.5); neither of these mutants suppressed the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), but both provided some suppression of the cold intolerance defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), suggesting that they may be partially redundant with fld-1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Y48G8AL.13 and F41H10.5 mutants provided some suppression of the cold intolerance defect of the paqr-2 mutant.
source: There exist four other genes in C. elegans that are closely related to fld-1 (Figure 1E), and null mutants were available for two of them (Y48G8AL.13 and F41H10.5); neither of these mutants suppressed the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), but both provided some suppression of the cold intolerance defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), suggesting that they may be partially redundant with fld-1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by cold tolerance assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Y48G8AL.13 and F41H10.5 may be partially redundant with fld-1.
source: There exist four other genes in C. elegans that are closely related to fld-1 (Figure 1E), and null mutants were available for two of them (Y48G8AL.13 and F41H10.5); neither of these mutants suppressed the glucose intolerance of the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), but both provided some suppression of the cold intolerance defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), suggesting that they may be partially redundant with fld-1.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial suppression of cold intolerance by these mutants.

claim: fld-1(et48) greatly enhanced the suppression of paqr-2 mutant glucose intolerance by mdt-15(et14), cept-1(et10), and hacd-1(et12) mutations.
source: The fld-1(et48) mutation greatly enhanced the effect of the mdt-15(et14), cept-1(et10) and hacd-1(et12) mutations in supressing intolerance to glucose and, in the case of mdt-15(et14) and cept-1(et10), to the more severe membrane-rigidifying diet of palmitic acid (PA)-loaded E. coli (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: fld-1(et48) acts in a pathway separate from mdt-15, cept-1, and hacd-1.
source: This result strongly indicates that fld-1(et48) acts in a pathway separate from that of mdt-15 (a mediator subunit), cept-1 (a choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferase) and hacd-1 (a hydroxyl-acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), which promote membrane fluidity by activating FA desaturases (Svensk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects of fld-1 with these other mutations.

claim: mdt-15, cept-1, and hacd-1 promote membrane fluidity by activating FA desaturases.
source: This result strongly indicates that fld-1(et48) acts in a pathway separate from that of mdt-15 (a mediator subunit), cept-1 (a choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferase) and hacd-1 (a hydroxyl-acyl-CoA dehydrogenase), which promote membrane fluidity by activating FA desaturases (Svensk et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Svensk et al., 2013.

claim: fld-1(et48) restores membrane fluidity to paqr-2(tm3410) mutant worms cultivated in the presence of glucose or PA-loaded E. coli.
source: In vivo FRAP measurements confirm that the fld-1(et48) allele restores membrane fluidity to paqr-2(tm3410) mutant worms cultivated in the presence of glucose or PA-loaded E. coli (Figure 3A–B), and expression of the desaturase fat-7::GFP reporter was enhanced by mdt-15(et14) and cept-1(et10) but not by fld-1(et48) or fld-1(et49), again showing that fld-1 acts in a separate pathway (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: Expression of the desaturase fat-7::GFP reporter was enhanced by mdt-15(et14) and cept-1(et10) but not by fld-1(et48) or fld-1(et49).
source: In vivo FRAP measurements confirm that the fld-1(et48) allele restores membrane fluidity to paqr-2(tm3410) mutant worms cultivated in the presence of glucose or PA-loaded E. coli (Figure 3A–B), and expression of the desaturase fat-7::GFP reporter was enhanced by mdt-15(et14) and cept-1(et10) but not by fld-1(et48) or fld-1(et49), again showing that fld-1 acts in a separate pathway (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP reporter measurements shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: RNAi knockdown of fat-6 and/or fat-7 abolished the suppression of paqr-2(tm3410) glucose intolerance by fld-1(et48).
source: Interestingly, RNAi knockdown of the desaturases fat-6 and/or fat-7 abolished the suppression of paqr-2(tm3410) glucose intolerance by fld-1(et48), and this was the case both in the presence or absence of the mdt-15(et14) gof allele (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Knockdown of fat-5 abolished the suppression of paqr-2(tm3410) glucose intolerance by fld-1(et48) but not in the presence of mdt-15(et14).
source: Knockdown of the desaturase fat-5 also abolished the suppression of paqr-2(tm3410) glucose intolerance by fld-1(et48) but not in the presence of mdt-15(et14) which likely drives sufficient compensatory induction of fat-6 and fat-7.
evidence: This is demonstrated by RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: fld-1(et48) does not act by promoting increased desaturase expression but desaturase activity is important for its effect on membrane homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that fld-1(et48) does not act by promoting increased desaturase expression but that desaturase activity is important for its effect on membrane homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of desaturase upregulation but requirement for desaturase activity.

claim: Phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs) are the most abundant phospholipids in C. elegans.
source: Phosphatidylethanolamines (PEs) are the most abundant phospholipids in C. elegans (Dancy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dancy et al., 2015.

claim: The paqr-2(tm3410) mutant has an excess of SFAs and reduced levels of LCPUFAs in PEs when challenged with glucose.
source: An analysis of the PE composition in worms challenged with growth on glucose shows that the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant has an excess of SFAs and reduced levels of LCPUFAs, and that these defects are partially corrected by the mdt-15(et14) or fld-1(et48) mutations, and fully corrected by a combination of both these mutations (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The PE composition defects in paqr-2(tm3410) mutant are partially corrected by mdt-15(et14) or fld-1(et48) mutations, and fully corrected by a combination of both mutations.
source: An analysis of the PE composition in worms challenged with growth on glucose shows that the paqr-2(tm3410) mutant has an excess of SFAs and reduced levels of LCPUFAs, and that these defects are partially corrected by the mdt-15(et14) or fld-1(et48) mutations, and fully corrected by a combination of both these mutations (Figure 3F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 3F-G.

claim: The levels of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) were unchanged in the PEs of the fld-1 mutant, even in combination with the mdt-15(et14) mutation.
source: The levels of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) were unchanged in the PEs of the fld-1 mutant, even in combination with the mdt-15(et14) mutation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cholesterol does not appear to play a structural role in C. elegans but instead is a likely precursor for essential low-abundance metabolites.
source: Note that the lipidomic analysis was performed on whole worms, and thus reflects global lipid composition rather than the composition of any specific membrane; also, cholesterol levels were not measured since this lipid does not appear to play a structural role in C. elegans but instead is a likely precursor for essential low-abundance metabolites (Merris et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Merris et al., 2004.

claim: fld-1(et48) and mdt-15(et14) mutations do not cause excess membrane fluidity either by themselves or in combination.
source: Some mechanism likely exists to prevent excess membrane fluidity since the fld-1(et48) and mdt-15(et14) mutations do not cause an excess fluidity either by themselves or in combination in any of the tested conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some mechanism likely exists to prevent excess membrane fluidity.
source: Some mechanism likely exists to prevent excess membrane fluidity since the fld-1(et48) and mdt-15(et14) mutations do not cause an excess fluidity either by themselves or in combination in any of the tested conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that fld-1 and mdt-15 mutations do not cause excess fluidity.

claim: The fld-1 mutation suppresses the growth defect of the fat-2 mutant both on normal plates and plates containing 20 mM glucose.
source: We found that, indeed, the fld-1 mutation suppresses the growth defect of the fat-2 mutant both on normal plates and plates containing 20 mM glucose, even in a paqr-2(tm3410) mutant background (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by growth assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: The fld-1 mutation causes either increased production of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids or lowers their turnover.
source: We interpret these results to mean that the fld-1 mutation causes either increased production of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids or lowers their turnover; either effect therefore allows the abundance of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids to reach an increased level in membranes even if their production is reduced by mutations in paqr-2, iglr-2 or fat-2.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic interaction data.

claim: fld-1(et48) can suppress the inability of the paqr-2 mutant to accumulate exogenously provided EPA.
source: This interpretation is further supported by the observation that fld-1(et48) can suppress the inability of the paqr-2 mutant to accumulate the exogenously provided LCPUFAs eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA; 20:5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D); notably, this demonstrates that no synthesis of LCPUFAs is required for fld-1(et48) to promote their accumulation among phospholipids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: No synthesis of LCPUFAs is required for fld-1(et48) to promote their accumulation among phospholipids.
source: This interpretation is further supported by the observation that fld-1(et48) can suppress the inability of the paqr-2 mutant to accumulate the exogenously provided LCPUFAs eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA; 20:5) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D); notably, this demonstrates that no synthesis of LCPUFAs is required for fld-1(et48) to promote their accumulation among phospholipids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the EPA supplementation experiment.

claim: TLCD1 is most strongly expressed in heart, muscle, liver and fat in mouse.
source: The mouse and human TLCD1 and TLCD2 genes are expressed in a variety of tissues, with heart, muscle, liver and fat being strongest for TLCD1 and heart, muscle, liver, small intestine and fat being strongest for the more variably expressed TLCD2 (Fagerberg et al., 2014) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fagerberg et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: TLCD2 is most strongly expressed in heart, muscle, liver, small intestine and fat in mouse.
source: The mouse and human TLCD1 and TLCD2 genes are expressed in a variety of tissues, with heart, muscle, liver and fat being strongest for TLCD1 and heart, muscle, liver, small intestine and fat being strongest for the more variably expressed TLCD2 (Fagerberg et al., 2014) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fagerberg et al., 2014 and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of TLCD1 or TLCD2 using siRNA in human HEK293 cells has little effect under normal conditions.
source: The molecular function of these proteins in mammals appears conserved with that of the C. elegans fld-1: knockdown of either gene using siRNA in human HEK293 cells has little effect on these cells under normal conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D) but was protective against the membrane rigidifying effects of PA (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E); knockdown of the control gene PPIB had no effect on membrane fluidity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Knockdown of TLCD1 or TLCD2 was protective against the membrane rigidifying effects of PA in HEK293 cells.
source: The molecular function of these proteins in mammals appears conserved with that of the C. elegans fld-1: knockdown of either gene using siRNA in human HEK293 cells has little effect on these cells under normal conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D) but was protective against the membrane rigidifying effects of PA (Figure 4A–B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E); knockdown of the control gene PPIB had no effect on membrane fluidity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Knockdown of TLCD1 or TLCD2 protected HEK293 cells from PA-induced apoptosis.
source: Importantly, knockdown of TLCD1 and TLCD2 also protected the HEK293 cells from PA-induced apoptosis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by apoptosis assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H-I.

claim: TLCD1 and TLCD2 do not regulate the uptake of exogenous SFAs.
source: TLCD1 and TLCD2 do not regulate the uptake of exogenous SFAs since there is no difference in the uptake rate of labelled PA in HEK293 cells treated with siRNA against either gene (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by PA uptake assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2J.

claim: The SFA content in the TAGs of PA-treated HEK293 cells is unaffected by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown.
source: The SFA content in the TAGs of PA-treated HEK293 cells is also unaffected by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K), as is their TAG/PC ratio (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L) and Nile red staining of lipid stores (Figure 4—figure supplement 2M–N), suggesting no effect on either uptake or sequestering of FAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K.

claim: TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown does not affect TAG/PC ratio in PA-treated HEK293 cells.
source: The SFA content in the TAGs of PA-treated HEK293 cells is also unaffected by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K), as is their TAG/PC ratio (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L) and Nile red staining of lipid stores (Figure 4—figure supplement 2M–N), suggesting no effect on either uptake or sequestering of FAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2L.

claim: TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown does not affect Nile red staining of lipid stores in PA-treated HEK293 cells.
source: The SFA content in the TAGs of PA-treated HEK293 cells is also unaffected by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K), as is their TAG/PC ratio (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L) and Nile red staining of lipid stores (Figure 4—figure supplement 2M–N), suggesting no effect on either uptake or sequestering of FAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by Nile red staining shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2M-N.

claim: TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown does not affect uptake or sequestering of FAs.
source: The SFA content in the TAGs of PA-treated HEK293 cells is also unaffected by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K), as is their TAG/PC ratio (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L) and Nile red staining of lipid stores (Figure 4—figure supplement 2M–N), suggesting no effect on either uptake or sequestering of FAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of changes in TAG content and lipid stores.

claim: The expression levels of the desaturases SCD and FADS1-3 are not increased by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown.
source: The expression levels of the desaturases SCD and FADS1-3 are also not increased by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2O) ruling this out as a mechanism for the fluidizing effect; indeed, the SCD expression is downregulated in TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown which may reflect a decreased demand on their activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2O.

claim: SCD expression is downregulated in TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown.
source: The expression levels of the desaturases SCD and FADS1-3 are also not increased by TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 2O) ruling this out as a mechanism for the fluidizing effect; indeed, the SCD expression is downregulated in TLCD1 or TLCD2 knockdown which may reflect a decreased demand on their activity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2O.

claim: TLCD1 knockdown causes a marked increase in the abundance of 18:2, 20:5 and 22:6 LCPUFAs in the PEs.
source: This conclusion is supported by the marked increase in the abundance of the 18:2, 20:5 and 22:6 LCPUFAs in the PEs of TLCD1 knockdown cells, and of the 18:2, 18:3 and 20:5 LCPUFAs in the PCs of TLCD2 knockdown cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TLCD2 knockdown causes an increase in the abundance of 18:2, 18:3 and 20:5 LCPUFAs in the PCs.
source: This conclusion is supported by the marked increase in the abundance of the 18:2, 20:5 and 22:6 LCPUFAs in the PEs of TLCD1 knockdown cells, and of the 18:2, 18:3 and 20:5 LCPUFAs in the PCs of TLCD2 knockdown cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cultivating HEK293 cells in the presence of exogenous EPA leads to its excess accumulation in PCs and PEs when TLCD2 is knocked down.
source: Cultivating HEK293 cells in the presence of exogenous EPA leads to its excess accumulation in PCs and PEs when TLCD2 is knocked down (Figure 4D–E), which demonstrates that, as in C. elegans, de novo PUFA synthesis is not required for the TLCD2 effect on PUFA-containing phospholipids; no change in TAG storage or EPA storage in TAGs occurred upon TLCD2 knockdown, indicating that TLCD2 does not regulate fatty acid storage or LCPUFA uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 3I–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: De novo PUFA synthesis is not required for the TLCD2 effect on PUFA-containing phospholipids.
source: Cultivating HEK293 cells in the presence of exogenous EPA leads to its excess accumulation in PCs and PEs when TLCD2 is knocked down (Figure 4D–E), which demonstrates that, as in C. elegans, de novo PUFA synthesis is not required for the TLCD2 effect on PUFA-containing phospholipids; no change in TAG storage or EPA storage in TAGs occurred upon TLCD2 knockdown, indicating that TLCD2 does not regulate fatty acid storage or LCPUFA uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 3I–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the EPA supplementation experiment.

claim: TLCD2 does not regulate fatty acid storage or LCPUFA uptake.
source: Cultivating HEK293 cells in the presence of exogenous EPA leads to its excess accumulation in PCs and PEs when TLCD2 is knocked down (Figure 4D–E), which demonstrates that, as in C. elegans, de novo PUFA synthesis is not required for the TLCD2 effect on PUFA-containing phospholipids; no change in TAG storage or EPA storage in TAGs occurred upon TLCD2 knockdown, indicating that TLCD2 does not regulate fatty acid storage or LCPUFA uptake (Figure 4—figure supplement 3I–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3I-J.

claim: As little as 1 μM of EPA or DHA prevents membrane rigidification by 400 μM PA in HEK293 cells.
source: The effect of TLCD2 knockdown on phospholipid EPA levels is especially interesting since LCPUFAs are very potent fluidizing lipids (Yang et al., 2011), which we confirmed experimentally in our cell system where as little as 1 μM of EPA or docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) prevents membrane rigidification by 400 μM PA (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: LCPUFAs are very potent fluidizing lipids.
source: The effect of TLCD2 knockdown on phospholipid EPA levels is especially interesting since LCPUFAs are very potent fluidizing lipids (Yang et al., 2011), which we confirmed experimentally in our cell system where as little as 1 μM of EPA or docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) prevents membrane rigidification by 400 μM PA (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2011 and confirmed by experimental data in Figure 4F-G.

claim: TLCD2 knockdown caused increased incorporation of LA in PCs and PEs within 6 hr of incubation.
source: The results show that TLCD2 knockdown caused increased incorporation of LA in PCs and PEs within 6 hr of incubation, and that increased incorporation was also evident by 24 hr in the PEs of TLCD1 and TLCD2 knockdown cells (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 13C-labeled LA incorporation experiments shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: Increased LA incorporation was evident by 24 hr in the PEs of TLCD1 and TLCD2 knockdown cells.
source: The results show that TLCD2 knockdown caused increased incorporation of LA in PCs and PEs within 6 hr of incubation, and that increased incorporation was also evident by 24 hr in the PEs of TLCD1 and TLCD2 knockdown cells (Figure 4H–I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 13C-labeled LA incorporation experiments shown in Figure 4H-I.

claim: No obvious differences were observed in TLCD1/2 knockdown cells during the chase part of the LA incorporation experiment.
source: No obvious differences were observed in the TLCD1/2 knockdown cells during the chase part of the experiment (Figure 4—figure supplement 3K–L).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the chase experiment shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3K-L.

claim: The primary function of TLCD1 and TLCD2 is to limit the formation of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids rather than promote their turnover.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the primary function of TLCD1 and TLCD2 is to limit the formation of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids rather than promote their turnover.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased incorporation but no change in turnover of labeled LA.

claim: TLCD2 siRNA protects against the potentiated rigidifying effects of PA when the FADS2 desaturase is knocked down.
source: Firstly, we found that TLCD2 siRNA protects against the potentiated rigidifying effects of PA when the FADS2 desaturase is knocked down (Figure 4J–K; Figure 4—figure supplement 3M), just as the fld-1 mutation suppressed the effects of the fat-2 mutation in C. elegans; this also strengthens the conclusion that TLCD2 acts independently from the desaturases.
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 4J-K.

claim: TLCD2 acts independently from the desaturases.
source: Firstly, we found that TLCD2 siRNA protects against the potentiated rigidifying effects of PA when the FADS2 desaturase is knocked down (Figure 4J–K; Figure 4—figure supplement 3M), just as the fld-1 mutation suppressed the effects of the fat-2 mutation in C. elegans; this also strengthens the conclusion that TLCD2 acts independently from the desaturases.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of TLCD2 knockdown to suppress effects even when desaturases are knocked down.

claim: TLCD2 knockdown suppresses membrane rigidification in HEK293 cells where AdipoR2 had been knocked down.
source: We also found that TLCD2 knockdown suppresses membrane rigidification in HEK293 cells where AdipoR2 had been knocked down, which by itself increases the sensitivity to the effect of PA on membrane rigidification (Devkota et al., 2017) (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: AdipoR2 knockdown increases the sensitivity to the effect of PA on membrane rigidification.
source: We also found that TLCD2 knockdown suppresses membrane rigidification in HEK293 cells where AdipoR2 had been knocked down, which by itself increases the sensitivity to the effect of PA on membrane rigidification (Devkota et al., 2017) (Figure 5A–B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Devkota et al., 2017.

claim: TLCD2 knockdown causes a strong increase in the levels of EPA in PCs.
source: As noted earlier, TLCD2 knockdown causes a strong increase in the levels of EPA in PCs (Figure 4C), which is a potent fluidizing LCPUFA: 5 μM are sufficient to completely protect AdipoR2 knockdown cells from the rigidifying effects of 200 μM PA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 5 μM EPA is sufficient to completely protect AdipoR2 knockdown cells from the rigidifying effects of 200 μM PA.
source: As noted earlier, TLCD2 knockdown causes a strong increase in the levels of EPA in PCs (Figure 4C), which is a potent fluidizing LCPUFA: 5 μM are sufficient to completely protect AdipoR2 knockdown cells from the rigidifying effects of 200 μM PA (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by FRAP measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: TLCD1 and TLCD2 siRNA improved the UFA content of PCs and PEs in AdipoR2 knockdown cells treated with 200 μM PA.
source: TLCD2 knockdown also suppresses the composition defect in HEK293 cells where AdipoR2 had been knocked down: TLCD1 and TLCD2 siRNA both improved the UFA content of PCs and PEs in AdipoR2 knockdown cells treated with 200 μM PA (Figure 5D–E), and also normalized ceramide levels in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: TLCD1 and TLCD2 siRNA normalized ceramide levels in AdipoR2 knockdown cells treated with PA.
source: TLCD2 knockdown also suppresses the composition defect in HEK293 cells where AdipoR2 had been knocked down: TLCD1 and TLCD2 siRNA both improved the UFA content of PCs and PEs in AdipoR2 knockdown cells treated with 200 μM PA (Figure 5D–E), and also normalized ceramide levels in these cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 are distantly related to the ER-localized ceramide synthases and translocation associated membrane proteins.
source: Structurally, the FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 proteins are characterized by the presence of a TLC domain and are therefore distantly related to the ER-localized ceramide synthases (human CERS1-6) and to the translocation associated membrane proteins (human TRAM1, TRAM2 and TRAM1L1) involved in membrane protein synthesis in the rough ER (Pewzner-Jung et al., 2006; Winter and Ponting, 2002).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and supported by citations.

claim: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 are localized to the plasma membrane rather than in the ER.
source: In contrast to the CERSs and TRAMs, FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 are localized to the plasma membrane rather than in the ER (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4) (Papanayotou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data and supported by a citation.

claim: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 are neither ceramide synthases nor translocation associated proteins.
source: This, and the fact that they lack critical motifs, indicate that FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 are neither ceramide synthases nor translocation associated proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from their localization and lack of critical motifs.

claim: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 act at the level of the plasma membrane by limiting the amounts of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids.
source: Instead, their localization and effect on PUFA content in membrane phospholipids suggest that they act at the level of the plasma membrane by limiting the amounts of LCPUFA-containing phospholipids.
evidence: This is inferred from their localization and effects on lipid composition.

claim: FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 may influence substrate selection by phospholipases or lysophospholipid acyltransferases.
source: It is possible, for example, that FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 influence substrate selection by phospholipases or lysophospholipid acyltransferases, that is regulating the Lands cycle through which phospholipids are actively remodelled by fatty acid exchange and hence effectively influence membrane composition and properties (Shindou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of action, supported by a citation.

claim: The plasma membrane localisation of FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 makes a direct control of lysophospholipid acyltransferases rather unlikely.
source: Note however that the plasma membrane localisation of FLD-1 and TLCD1/2 makes a direct control of lysophospholipid acyltransferases, which are believed to localize in internal membranes, notably the ER, rather unlikely.
evidence: This is inferred from the different subcellular localizations.

claim: LCPUFAs can serve as precursors for many signalling lipids.
source: The type of LCPUFAs that are elevated in the C. elegans fld-1 mutant and in HEK293 treated with siRNA against TLCD1/2 could have other effects besides influencing membrane fluidity. In particular LCPUFAs can serve as precursors for many signalling lipids (Funk, 2001; Watts, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Funk, 2001 and Watts, 2016.

claim: fld-1 has its primary effects on membrane fluidity.
source: That fld-1 has its primary effects on membrane fluidity is however supported by several lines of evidence, much of which hinges on the fact that fld-1 mutants act as paqr-2 and iglr-2 suppressors.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including genetic interactions and FRAP measurements.

claim: The paqr-2 and iglr-2 mutants have membrane fluidity defects.
source: This is important because the paqr-2 and iglr-2 mutants clearly have membrane fluidity defects since: a) They are sensitive to membrane-rigidifying conditions (cold or exogenous SFAs); b) Their mutant phenotypes are suppressed by other mutations that promote an increase in fluidizing UFAs, by exogenous UFAs or by fluidizing amounts of mild detergents (NP-40 or Triton X-100); c) The paqr-2 and iglr-2 mutants have an excess of membrane-rigidifying SFA-containing phospholipids; and d) The paqr-2 and iglr-2 phenotypes are closely associated with reduced membrane fluidity measured in vivo using FRAP under numerous different experimental conditions or genotypes (Devkota et al., 2017; Svensk et al., 2016a; Svensk et al., 2013; Svensson et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence and citations to previous work.

claim: The effect of TLCD1/2 on plasma membrane composition likely explains the published observations that TLCD1 facilitates the activity of calcium channels that are essential during neural plate development.
source: The effect of TLCD1/2 on plasma membrane composition likely explains the published observations that TLCD1 facilitates the activity of calcium channels that are essential during neural plate development (Papanayotou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to previous observations, supported by a citation.

claim: Membrane composition can have strong effects on insulin secretion by beta cells, glucose transport, endocytosis, regulation of metabolic rate, platelet aggregation and TRPV channel activity.
source: Indeed, membrane composition can have strong effects on a variety of processes including insulin secretion by beta cells (MacDonald et al., 2015), glucose transport (Ginsberg et al., 1982), endocytosis (Krischer et al., 1993; Illinger et al., 1991), regulation of metabolic rate (Hulbert and Else, 2000), platelet aggregation (Winocour et al., 1990) and TRPV channel activity (Caires et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: PUFAs are readily peroxidized.
source: Conversely, given the chemical instability of PUFAs, which are readily peroxidized (Gaschler and Stockwell, 2017; Ayala et al., 2014; Kelley et al., 2014; Catalá, 2013), it seems natural for cells to have mechanisms that limit their levels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It seems natural for cells to have mechanisms that limit PUFA levels.
source: Conversely, given the chemical instability of PUFAs, which are readily peroxidized (Gaschler and Stockwell, 2017; Ayala et al., 2014; Kelley et al., 2014; Catalá, 2013), it seems natural for cells to have mechanisms that limit their levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chemical instability of PUFAs.

claim: The C. elegans fld-1 mutant exhibits an enhanced oxidative stress response when challenged with LA.
source: Indeed, we found that the C. elegans fld-1 mutant exhibits an enhanced oxidative stress response when challenged with the LCPUFA LA (Figure 1—figure supplement 6J–L), which indicates a function for fld-1 in preventing such PUFA-derived oxidative stress.
evidence: This is demonstrated by gst-4::GFP reporter measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6J-L.

claim: fld-1 has a function in preventing PUFA-derived oxidative stress.
source: Indeed, we found that the C. elegans fld-1 mutant exhibits an enhanced oxidative stress response when challenged with the LCPUFA LA (Figure 1—figure supplement 6J–L), which indicates a function for fld-1 in preventing such PUFA-derived oxidative stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced oxidative stress response in the mutant.

claim: The ubiquitous plasma membrane expression of C. elegans fld-1 suggests that it functions in most cells.
source: The ubiquitous plasma membrane expression of C. elegans fld-1 suggests that it functions in most cells, though it is not required under non-challenging conditions given the relative health of the mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the expression pattern and lack of obvious phenotypes in the single mutant.

claim: fld-1 is not required under non-challenging conditions.
source: The ubiquitous plasma membrane expression of C. elegans fld-1 suggests that it functions in most cells, though it is not required under non-challenging conditions given the relative health of the mutant.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of obvious phenotypes in the single mutant under normal conditions.

claim: A function of paqr-2 and iglr-2 in C. elegans is to prevent SFA lipotoxicity.
source: The present work further establishes that a function of paqr-2 and iglr-2 in C. elegans is to prevent SFA lipotoxicity, and specifically to prevent membrane rigidification by SFAs, and further suggests that they may act via two separate pathways: 1) Upregulation of desaturases to promote membrane fluidity; and 2) Inhibition of fld-1 directly or of a fld-1-regulated pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current work and previous studies.

claim: paqr-2 and iglr-2 may act via two separate pathways: upregulation of desaturases and inhibition of fld-1 or a fld-1-regulated pathway.
source: The present work further establishes that a function of paqr-2 and iglr-2 in C. elegans is to prevent SFA lipotoxicity, and specifically to prevent membrane rigidification by SFAs, and further suggests that they may act via two separate pathways: 1) Upregulation of desaturases to promote membrane fluidity; and 2) Inhibition of fld-1 directly or of a fld-1-regulated pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the existence of two classes of paqr-2 suppressors.

claim: There are two classes of paqr-2 suppressors: mutations that activate desaturases and loss-of-function mutations in fld-1.
source: This conclusion is supported by the existence of two classes of paqr-2 suppressors: mutations that activate desaturases (e.g. gof mutations in nhr-49 or mdt-15, and lof mutations in sams-1, cept-1, pcyt-1, ech-7 or hacd-1) (Svensk et al., 2013) and loss-of-function mutations in fld-1, which does not act by upregulating desaturases though it depends on their activity (present work).
evidence: This is based on the genetic screen results and characterization of suppressors.

claim: paqr-2 may influence fld-1 activity.
source: The suggestion that paqr-2 may influence fld-1 activity is raised only as a possibility consistent with the observed genetic interactions; we have at present no biochemical evidence that these proteins interact with each other nor do we know of a mechanism by which paqr-2 could regulate fld-1.
evidence: This is speculation based on genetic interactions, with explicit acknowledgment of lack of biochemical evidence.

claim: Inhibitors of TLCD1/2 may have therapeutic potential in instances of lipotoxicity and excess membrane rigidity.
source: We propose that inhibitors of TLCD1/2 may have therapeutic potential in instances of lipotoxicity and excess membrane rigidity, which is a feature of the diabetic condition (Pilon, 2016; Perona, 2017), or in instances of mutations in AdipoR1 that cause retina defects (Zhang et al., 2016; Rice et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposal for therapeutic application based on the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Excess membrane rigidity is a feature of the diabetic condition.
source: We propose that inhibitors of TLCD1/2 may have therapeutic potential in instances of lipotoxicity and excess membrane rigidity, which is a feature of the diabetic condition (Pilon, 2016; Perona, 2017), or in instances of mutations in AdipoR1 that cause retina defects (Zhang et al., 2016; Rice et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pilon, 2016 and Perona, 2017.

claim: Mutations in AdipoR1 cause retina defects.
source: We propose that inhibitors of TLCD1/2 may have therapeutic potential in instances of lipotoxicity and excess membrane rigidity, which is a feature of the diabetic condition (Pilon, 2016; Perona, 2017), or in instances of mutations in AdipoR1 that cause retina defects (Zhang et al., 2016; Rice et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2016 and Rice et al., 2015.

claim: Inhibition of the mammalian TLCD1/2 homologs may be well tolerated.
source: Encouragingly, we found that the fld-1 C. elegans single mutant has no obvious phenotype, which suggests that inhibition of the mammalian homologs may be well tolerated.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of obvious phenotypes in the C. elegans fld-1 mutant.
